title: From Bikaner to Baker Street: London Crowns the First Global Indian Restaurant Award Winners
excerpt: Sanjeev Kapoor, Atul Kochhar, and the Cinnamon Club headline an inaugural ceremony that finally treats Indian dining abroad as a global industry, not a niche.
body:
For decades, Indian restaurants outside India existed in a strange purgatory — beloved by locals, ignored by the industry's formal recognition apparatus. The inaugural Indian Restaurant Congress & Awards in London, held on May 28 at the Royal Lancaster Hotel, set out to change that. By most accounts, it succeeded.

The event, organised by the Indian Restaurant Congress after 14 years of running a domestic version, brought 250 restaurateurs, chefs, and hospitality executives from across Europe, Asia, and the subcontinent to a single room. The goal was straightforward: build a credible, international awards platform for Indian cuisine — something the sector has lacked even as Indian restaurants have multiplied in virtually every Western capital.

## The winners

The awards jury — which included BBC journalist George Shaw, critic Andy Hayler, and celebrated TV host Rashmi Uday Singh — announced 15 categories of winners. The headliners were unmistakable.

**Sanjeev Kapoor** took home the Global Indian Chef of the Year award, a recognition of his influence well beyond the kitchen. **Atul Kochhar**, the pioneering twice Michelin-starred chef from Jamshedpur who changed how Britain perceives Indian food, received the Culinary Excellence Award. **The Cinnamon Club**, Vivek Singh's Westminster institution that has served parliamentarians and prime ministers since 2001, was named Global Indian Restaurant of the Year.

Other notable winners included **Jamavar** (Best Indian Restaurant Brand), **Tresind** (Restaurant Group of the Year), **Kahani** (Best Fine Dining Indian Restaurant), **Colonel Saab** (Best Indian Restaurant – United Kingdom), and **Kutir** (Critics' Choice Indian Restaurant). Café Spice Namasté, Cyrus Todiwala's long-standing East London favourite, received the Culinary Heritage Award — a fitting nod to a chef who holds both an OBE and a loyal following that spans generations of British diners.

## Why this matters for the diaspora

The conference sessions, led by speakers including Vivek Singh, Anjan Chatterjee, and Romy Gill MBE, focused on themes that resonate far beyond London: scaling culinary brands globally, adapting to evolving consumer palates, and making the business case for Indian fine dining in markets that still sometimes conflate the cuisine with £7.99 takeaway deals.

For the roughly three million Indians in the UK — and millions more across the Gulf, North America, and Southeast Asia — the event signals a shift. Indian dining abroad is no longer just a fragmented collection of family-run curry houses. It is an industry with institutional ambition, cross-border investment flows, and a growing appetite for formal recognition.

The organisers have already announced plans for a second edition. If the inaugural ceremony is any indication, the global Indian restaurant scene is done waiting for a seat at the table. It is building its own.

*Sources: Restaurant India, Good Curry Guide, Atul Kochhar official website*
